verdict.reasoning: Patient reports dizziness starting about two hours ago and that it has been continuous: “Started probably about two hours ago…”, and when asked if it is there continuously: “Yeah it's, it's there, the whole time… So it's there now for the past two hours you'd say, yeah? – Yep.”

Sudden onset dizziness with room spinning, unsteadiness, and ear buzzing are all described: “I just suddenly felt very fuzzy and dizzy, um, and a bit shaky.”; “the the room is sort of spinning”; “I can't walk properly… not straight”; “and my ears are buzzing a bit.”
Nausea without vomiting is documented: “Have you been physically sick? – No, but now I'm feeling very sick. – Nausea, OK.” No vomiting is reported.
Prior similar brief episode is described: “I had a a similar sort of thing about a month ago… it settled quite quickly.” When asked how long it lasted: “Probably only about five, ten minutes.”

Transcript confirms absence of these features: no limb weakness (“My, my legs and arms and everything are working fine… – So there's no weakness of your arms and legs. OK. – No.”), no hearing loss (“do you have any problems hearing…? – No… I can hear everything.”), no ear pain/discharge (“Any kind of ear pain or ear discharge…? – No, nothing.”), no recent viral/URI (“Did you have any kind of viral illness…? – No.”; “No cold, cough, nothing.”), and no fever (“Do you have a temperature at all? – I don't think so…”).
Past medical history explicitly states: “Um, I've had premature ovarian failure…”
HRT use is documented: “I've had premature ovarian failure, um, and I've taken HRT.”
Allergies are specifically denied: “OK, do you have any allergies at all? – No.” This supports no known drug allergies.
Acute vertigo and likely labyrinthitis are stated: symptoms are acute (“Started probably about two hours ago”), and doctor says, “the most common… diagnosis… is something called labyrinthitis.”

Doctor prescribes vestibular suppressant (unnamed) at stated dose and duration to Lloyds Pharmacy: “we'll start you on certain medications… it's called , yeah? It's one tablet three times a day. So I'll give you about ten days worth.” and “I'll send the a prescription… looks like it's the Lloyd pharmacy on our system. Is that correct? – Yeah. – Yeah. So we'll send you across that prescription.”

In-person assessment plan is clear: “I would still like you to be seen by one of our doctors to take a look inside your ears… while you're with the doctors, we'd like to do your blood pressure, just examine your, you know, you know, how your walking and everything is.” This corresponds to otoscopy, BP, and neuro/gait evaluation.

Safety-net advice is explicitly given: “if you double up any weakness of your legs or arms or, or, you know, a sudden headache… or you start being violently sick with it, then… you would need to take your to A and E.” This matches limb weakness, severe headache, or persistent vomiting as reasons to go to A&E.
Patient is told to contact support to book the appointment: “Just make sure you call support to book that appointment, OK? – I will, thank you very much.”
